podcast.title: Berkeley College of Music Education
podcast.body: Furthered his musical education by studying bass at the prestigious Berkeley in Boston. "You went to Berkeley, right? Yeah, eventually. Berkeley, Aboston, yeah, to study bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Musical Education Through Trent Carr
podcast.body: With few other friends, White spent weekends at Trent Carr's downtown Toronto home, receiving his "musical rock and roll education." Carr would play him records by bands like Led Zeppelin and The Who, inspiring White to practice bass alone throughout the week. "He'd play me like, let's out on a pink floor and the who and all these bands. And then I'd go home and play bass all week by myself and then come back and show him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Scarborough Upbringing
podcast.body: Grew up in Scarborough, Ontario, which he characterized as a "cultural wasteland" due to a lack of local musical scene or friends outside of Trent Carr. "I grew up in Scarborough, which was a cultural wasteland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Trent Carr's Influence on Becoming a Bassist
podcast.body: Became a bass player because his childhood friend Trent Carr advised him to. When White expressed interest in buying a guitar, Carr told him he should get a bass instead, a suggestion White readily accepted. "The only reason I'm a bass player is because I was, I've known Trent since I was really young... Trent said, no, you should get a bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Childhood Friend and Musical Influence on Tim White
xref.body: Carr has known Tim White since childhood and played a pivotal role in White's musical journey. He suggested White buy a bass instead of a guitar, and later provided White's "musical rock and roll education" by exposing him to bands like Led Zeppelin and The Who, fostering White's development as a bassist. "Trent said, no, you should get a bass. I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, okay. Yeah."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hugh Dillon's Recovery Journey
xref.body: Hugh Dillon's recovery from addiction was a long and arduous process, supported primarily by his wife Midori, manager Bernie Brin, and bandmates Tim White and Trent Carr, who never gave up on him. He underwent multiple rehab and detox programs, eventually reaching a point of honesty that enabled change. "My wife, my family, my wife is the, Midori is the prime mover and all of it because she never, and like these guys, and this is why I go back to the people behind the scenes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

xref.title: Hugh's Producing Role and Band Dynamics
xref.body: As a lyricist and singer who took on a producing role, Hugh Dillon often struggled to articulate musical problems, relying on Tim White's ability to "disassemble a song" and Trent Carr's natural, "painter-like" talent, despite the frustration of trying to capture specific takes. "I'm a lyricist and a singer. I don't have the same skill set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 2

xref.title: Subconscious Noodling Songwriting Method
xref.body: The band's songwriting often begins with Trent Carr or Tim White "noodling" subconsciously during live performances or jams. Hugh Dillon actively listens for these spontaneous musical ideas, isolating specific notes or riffs that he finds unique and then developing them into full songs, rather than deliberately trying to write "hits." "I'll hear them subconsciously noodle. And that's when I stop everybody and what's that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tim White's Post-Breakup Career
xref.body: Following the Headstones' breakup, Tim White continued his career in the recording business, leveraging his expertise as a musician. "Tim's been in the recording business since since I didn't write away right away."
